identity.title: Does the HCN/CO Ratio Trace the Star-forming Fraction of Gas? I. A Comparison with Analytical Models of Star Formation

paper_type_evidence.quote: We use archival ALMA observations of the HCN and CO $J=1-0$ transitions, in addition to the radio continuum at 93 GHz, to assess the relationship between dense gas, star formation, and gas dynamics in ten, nearby (U)LIRGs and late-type galaxy centers.
For each galaxy, we image archival ALMA data of the HCN, CN, CO, and HCO$^+$ $J=1-0$ transitions, in addition to the radio continuum emission at 93 GHz.

analysis_steps.goal: Reduce and image archival ALMA data and produce moment maps

method.value: Image archival ALMA data of HCN, CN, CO, and HCO+ J=1-0 and 93 GHz continuum with uv-matching and tapering to a common beam per galaxy (following Wilson et al. 2022, and re-imaging NGC 4038/9, NGC 1808, and NGC 3351 at higher velocity resolution). Generate integrated intensity (Moment 0) and velocity dispersion (Moment 2) maps of CO and HCN J=1-0 using Spectral Cube with a 5-sigma peak / 3-sigma wing mask.

evidence.quote: For each galaxy, we image archival ALMA data of the HCN, CN, CO, and HCO$^+$ $J=1-0$ transitions, in addition to the radio continuum emission at 93 GHz. The data are $uv-$matched and tapered to a common beam for each individual galaxy.
We produce maps of integrated intensity and velocity dispersion of the CO and HCN $J=1-0$ transitions using the Astropy Spectral Cube package (cite: Ginsburg:2019).

Masks are expanded around these peaks down to channels with emission at a SNR of three.
Emission from regions smaller than a beam area are masked.

key_parameters.value: Pixel selection cuts: SNR > 3 in integrated intensity and SNR > 2 in velocity dispersion

analysis_steps.goal: Derive molecular gas surface densities and dense gas fraction

method.value: Convert CO and HCN integrated intensities into total and dense molecular gas surface densities (Sigma_mol and Sigma_mol,dense) and compute the observational dense gas fraction f_dense = (alpha_HCN / alpha_CO) * (I_HCN / I_CO).

evidence.quote: To calculate the molecular gas mass surface density, $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$, we use: $$\begin{equation} \label{eq:Sigma_mol} \Sigma_\mathrm{mol} = \alpha_\mathrm{mol}\ I_\mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{cos}(i). \end{equation}$$

If all of the above assumptions are true, then the fraction of dense gas traced by HCN/CO is given by: $$\begin{equation} f_\mathrm{dense} = \frac{\alpha_\mathrm{HCN}}{\alpha_\mathrm{CO}} \frac{I_\mathrm{HCN}}{I_\mathrm{CO}}. \end{equation}$$ with $\alpha_\mathrm{HCN}/\alpha_\mathrm{CO}=3.2$ implied from the above discussion.

key_parameters.value: alpha_CO = 1.1 M_sun (K km s^-1 pc^2)^-1 for the ALMA sample; alpha_CO = 4.35 M_sun (K km s^-1 pc^2)^-1 for EMPIRE sample

evidence.quote: For ease of comparison with other studies our fiducial value is $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}=1.1$ \[M$_\odot$ (K km s$^{-1}$ pc$^2$)$^{-1}$\] for our sample of galaxies, the (U)LIRG value including Helium (cite: Downes:1993)
We choose a fixed value of $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}=4.35$ \[M$_\odot$ (K km s$^{-1}$ pc$^2$)$^{-1}$\] for the EMPIRE sample of galaxies
Furthermore, by using $\alpha_\mathrm{HCN}/\alpha_\mathrm{CO}=3.2$ our plots of $f_\mathrm{dense}$ are a direct reflection of the HCN/CO ratio.

evidence.quote: We apply inclination angles only to the disk galaxies in this sample, as inclination angles are typically uncertain in mergers and (U)LIRGs.

evidence.quote: We do this assuming that the physical effects impacting $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ will impact $\alpha_\mathrm{HCN}$ in a similar way.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive star formation rate surface densities, depletion times, free-fall times, and star formation efficiencies

method.value: Calculate SFR surface density from 93 GHz continuum using the Murphy et al. (2011) composite thermal+non-thermal calibration (with a 10% dust subtraction and AGN masking), and from smoothed Spitzer 24 um maps using Rieke et al. (2009) for EMPIRE. Compute total and dense gas depletion times (t_dep = Sigma_mol / Sigma_SFR), free-fall times (t_ff), and star formation efficiency per free-fall time (epsilon_ff = t_ff / t_dep).

evidence.quote: We adopt fixed values for $\alpha_\mathrm{NT}=0.84$ and $T_\mathrm{e}=10^4$ K, and we use the composite calibration from (cite: Murphy:2011) which accounts for both thermal and non-thermal contributions to the SFR:
We use the star formation rate (SFR) and molecular gas surface densities to estimate the depletion time of the total (mol$\,=\,$CO) and dense (mol$\,=\,$HCN) molecular gas content:

The efficiency of the star-formation process is then estimated by comparing the observed depletion timescales with estimates of the free-fall time: $$\begin{equation} \epsilon_\mathrm{ff}=\frac{t_\mathrm{ff}}{t_\mathrm{dep}} \end{equation}$$

key_parameters.value: T_e = 10^4 K, alpha_NT = 0.84, nu = 93 GHz, 10% dust correction, 30% SFR uncertainty

assumptions.value: Fixed half line-of-sight cloud depth R = 100 pc for all galaxies to estimate volume density rho = Sigma_mol / R

analysis_steps.goal: Construct gravoturbulent analytical star formation model grids and compare to observations

method.value: Generate model grids for three gravoturbulent prescriptions (LN PN11, LN+PL B18, LN Fixed) over the observed Sigma_mol and sigma_v parameter space using the scaled Sun et al. (2018) empirical relation. Compute model Sigma_SFR, P_turb, t_dep, epsilon_ff, f_grav, f(n > 10^4.5 cm^-3), t_dep,grav, and t_dep,dense. Evaluate Spearman rank correlation coefficients for observed trends and compute chi^2 of data relative to the fiducial model that best fits the Kennicutt-Schmidt relation.

evidence.quote: To compare models with data from our sample, we create a sets of models for each of the three, unique prescriptions. We produce LN models over the $\sigma_\mathrm{v}^2/R-\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ parameter space that encompasses our data in Fig. [1](#fig:grid).

We consider fiducial models which correspond to the parameters that best fit the observed Kennicutt-Schmidt relationship (see Fig. [3](#fig:KS_plots)). For each model, we calculate the $\chi^2$ of the data relative to this fiducial model, and this value is shown in each panel.
We refer to Spearman rank coefficients as a measure of the strength and direction of correlations between two parameters.

results_numeric.quantity: Constant gas volume density threshold traced by HCN/CO ratio (n_SF)

evidence.quote: We confirm that the HCN/CO ratio is a tracer of gas above $n_\mathrm{SF}\approx10^{4.5}$ cm$^{-3}$, but the sub-kpc variations in HCN/CO do not universally track $f_\mathrm{grav}$.
In summary, the HCN/CO ratio is likely a reliable tracer of gas above a constant density, such as $n_\mathrm{SF}\approx10^{4.5}$ cm$^{-3}$, but not necessarily $f_\mathrm{grav}$.

findings_qualitative.value: Observed f_dense (proportional to I_HCN/I_CO) shows a weak positive correlation with turbulent pressure P_turb, which matches model predictions for the gas fraction above a fixed density f(n > 10^4.5 cm^-3) rather than the self-gravitating gas fraction f_grav.

evidence.loc: Does HCN/CO trace the Star-forming Gas Fraction?
evidence.quote: From this result, the observed positive trend in $I_\mathrm{HCN}/I_\mathrm{CO}$ with $P_\mathrm{turb}$ is more consistent with $I_\mathrm{HCN}/I_\mathrm{CO}$ being a better tracer of $f(n>10^{4.5}$ cm$^{-3})$ than $f_\mathrm{grav}$.

findings_qualitative.value: Star formation efficiency per free-fall time (epsilon_ff) shows a weak negative correlation with P_turb and a weak positive correlation with f_dense across the sample.

evidence.loc: The Star Formation Efficiency per Free-fall Time

findings_qualitative.value: Total molecular gas depletion time (t_dep) shows moderate negative correlations with both f_dense and P_turb.

evidence.quote: We find moderate negative correlations between $t_\mathrm{dep}$ and the dense gas fraction traced by $I_\mathrm{HCN}/I_\mathrm{CO}$. $t_\mathrm{dep}$ estimated from the data appears relatively constant with $P_\mathrm{turb}$, but the Spearman rank coefficient of the combined data indicates a moderate, negative correlation (cf. Fig. [8](#fig:tdep_data)).

findings_qualitative.value: Dense gas depletion time (t_dep,dense) shows a weak positive correlation with f_dense in the combined dataset and a moderate positive correlation in ~3 sample sources and the EMPIRE galaxies.

evidence.quote: We see a moderate positive correlation between $t_\mathrm{dep,dense}$ and $f_\mathrm{dense}$ in $\sim$ 3 of our sources and the EMPIRE galaxies. The Spearman rank coefficient shows a weak, positive correlation for the combined dataset.

claims.hypothesis: The HCN/CO intensity ratio universally tracks the gravitationally-bound, star-forming gas fraction (f_grav) at sub-kpc scales in nearby galaxies.
claims.experiment: Compare observational estimates of f_dense (from ALMA HCN/CO J=1-0), P_turb (from CO linewidths and surface densities), epsilon_ff, t_dep, and t_dep,dense in 10 nearby (U)LIRGs and galaxy centers against predictions of f_grav and f(n > 10^4.5 cm^-3) from three gravoturbulent star formation models.
claims.result: Observed f_dense increases with P_turb, whereas varying-threshold models (LN PN11 and LN+PL B18) predict f_grav decreases with P_turb while f(n > 10^4.5 cm^-3) increases with P_turb; observed trends in epsilon_ff, t_dep, and t_dep,dense also match model trends with f(n > 10^4.5 cm^-3) rather than f_grav.
claims.finding: The HCN/CO ratio traces gas above a roughly constant density threshold (n_SF ~ 10^4.5 cm^-3), but sub-kpc variations in HCN/CO do not universally track f_grav.

evidence.quote: We confirm that the HCN/CO ratio is a tracer of gas above $n_\mathrm{SF}\approx10^{4.5}$ cm$^{-3}$, but the sub-kpc variations in HCN/CO do not universally track $f_\mathrm{grav}$.

We therefore conclude that the $I_\mathrm{HCN}/I_\mathrm{CO}$ ratio likely does not track $f_\mathrm{grav}$ as predicted by the varying-threshold models, but rather the fraction of gas above some fixed density, such as $f(n>10^{4.5}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3})$.

claims.hypothesis: Gravoturbulent star formation models with a varying star formation density threshold reproduce observed trends in depletion times (t_dep, t_dep,dense) and star formation efficiency (epsilon_ff) better than fixed density threshold models.
claims.experiment: Compare observed correlations of t_dep, t_dep,dense, and epsilon_ff with P_turb and f_dense against predictions from varying-threshold models (LN PN11 and LN+PL B18) and fixed-threshold models (LN Fixed).
claims.result: LN Fixed models predict a constant dense gas depletion time, a flattening of t_dep above P_turb ~ 10^7 K cm^-3, and a turnover in epsilon_ff with f_grav that are not seen in the data, whereas varying-threshold models reproduce the observed trends including the increase in t_dep,dense with f_dense.
claims.finding: Varying star formation density threshold models are strongly favored and better reproduce the average trends in our data and the EMPIRE sample compared to fixed-threshold models.

evidence.quote: We find strong evidence for the use of varying star formation density threshold models, which are able to reproduce trends observed in $t_\mathrm{dep}$ and $\epsilon_\mathrm{ff}$ that fixed threshold models cannot.

The varying-threshold models (lognormal+powerlaw B18 and lognormal-only PN11) are able to better reproduce the average trends of our data and the EMPIRE sample compared to the fixed-threshold lognormal-only models.

claims.hypothesis: Composite lognormal plus powerlaw (LN+PL) gas density PDF models outperform pure lognormal (LN) models in reproducing the observed trends and scatter in star formation properties.
claims.experiment: Compare predictions of the LN+PL B18 model across a range of powerlaw slopes (alpha_PL = 1.0-2.3) against pure lognormal LN PN11 models across a range of velocity dispersions.
claims.result: Variations in P_turb (or Mach number) in pure lognormal models fail to reproduce the vertical scatter in f_dense, epsilon_ff, t_dep, and t_dep,dense, whereas varying alpha_PL = 1.0-2.3 in the LN+PL B18 model reproduces both the average trends and the observed scatter.
claims.finding: Composite lognormal and powerlaw models outperform pure lognormal models, suggesting the scatter in star formation properties is driven in part by cloud evolution developing a self-gravitating powerlaw tail.

evidence.quote: Composite lognormal and powerlaw models outperform pure lognormal models in reproducing the observed trends, even when using a fixed powerlaw slope.
Out of the three models we consider, the LN+PL B18 models perform best at reproducing the observational trends and scatter of our data and the EMPIRE sample.

Variations in PL slope ($\alpha_\mathrm{PL}$) (lognormal+powerlaw B18 models) are able to explain the scatter in the data. The scatter in our data is not well-reproduced by variations in $P_\mathrm{turb}$ (or $\mathcal{M}$) alone.

why_this_data.value: To test the relationship between HCN/CO and f_grav in more extreme star-forming environments where turbulence is stronger (mergers, starbursts, (U)LIRGs, barred galaxy centers), complemented by the EMPIRE survey of normal galaxy disks.

evidence.quote: To assess the relationship between the HCN/CO ratio and $f_\mathrm{grav}$, we look to more extreme star-forming environments in which turbulence is stronger (e.g. mergers, starbursts, (U)LIRGs, barred galaxies).
We use the EMPIRE sample of galaxies (cite: Jimenez_Donaire:2019) as a comparison, which predominantly targets normal regions of star formation within galaxy disks.

why_this_method.value: In external galaxies where spatial resolution is limited, combining molecular line ratios of dense gas tracers (sensitive to n-PDF shape) with CO kinematic measurements (sensitive to Mach number and turbulent pressure) provides a tool to test gravoturbulent n-PDF models.

evidence.quote: In external galaxies where resolution is limited, molecular line ratios are an additional tool for assessing $n-$PDF shape.
Combining molecular line ratios of dense gas tracers with information on kinematics is therefore a promising tool for assessing $n-$PDF information of clouds in external galaxies.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Krumholz et al. (2012) prescriptions for free-fall time (t_ff) in the GMC and Toomre regimes were explored as an alternative to the fixed 100 pc line-of-sight depth prescription, yielding little qualitative difference.

evidence.quote: We also explored estimating free fall time using the (cite: Krumholz:2012) prescriptions for $t_\mathrm{ff}$ in the GMC and Toomre regimes. We find little qualitative difference in the results between using $t_\mathrm{ff}$ as described above and the (cite: Krumholz:2012) prescription.

limitations_admitted.value: Inclination angles are not applied to mergers and (U)LIRGs due to uncertainty, resulting in overestimates of Sigma_mol and other surface densities for systems with non-zero inclinations.

evidence.quote: We apply inclination angles only to the disk galaxies in this sample, as inclination angles are typically uncertain in mergers and (U)LIRGs. Thus, the uncorrected measurements of galaxies with non-zero inclinations will result in overestimates of $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ and other surface densities.

limitations_admitted.value: Fixed conversion factors (alpha_CO and alpha_HCN/alpha_CO = 3.2) are assumed, deferring pixel-by-pixel non-LTE radiative transfer modelling of emissivity and conversion factor variations to a companion paper.

evidence.quote: We do not directly assess variations in emissivity in this paper, and defer an analysis of emissivity (and therefore conversion factors) to (cite: Bemis:2020) and Bemis & Wilson, in prep., where we present modelling of the HCN and CO emissivities for our sample of galaxies on a pixel-by-pixel basis.

limitations_admitted.value: 93 GHz radio continuum SFR estimates are subject to ~30% uncertainty from variations in electron temperature (T_e), non-thermal spectral index (alpha_NT), and dust emissivity.

evidence.quote: We adopt this correction factor of $\sim10\%$ for all sources, but we acknowledge that the emissivity of dust at 93 GHz may vary between our sources.
We adopt an uncertainty of $30\%$ for SFR estimates derived from the radio continuum.

limitations_admitted.value: A fixed line-of-sight cloud depth of R = 100 pc is assumed for all galaxies when estimating mean volume density and free-fall time, which likely contributes to discrepancies between observed and modelled epsilon_ff vs. P_turb.

evidence.quote: We do not know $R$, so we assume a fixed value of 100 pc for all galaxies when estimating $\rho$.

The discrepancy between the models and data is likely in part due to inaccurate estimates of $t_\mathrm{ff}$ from our data. When estimating the mean density of the molecular gas traced by CO, we assume a fixed line-of-sight depth of 100 pc for all measurements

limitations_admitted.value: Using CO linewidths to trace cloud Mach number is limited by optical depth effects, disk rotation, large-scale motions, choice of fiducial sound speed (c_s = 0.4 km s^-1), and turbulent scale dependence across physical resolutions of ~50-900 pc.

evidence.loc: Velocity Dispersion as a Tracer of Mach Number
evidence.quote: There are limits to this approach, and the ability of the CO line to trace cloud turbulence may be limited by its optical depth (cite: Burkhart:2013; Goodman:2009), and observed line width can include disk rotation or other large-scale motions, but alternative measures of gas kinematics in extragalactic clouds are absent.
A sample of galaxies at different physical scales will therefore be affected by this scale dependence, such that velocity dispersions will be smaller at smaller scales and vice versa.

limitations_admitted.value: Variations in the relative beam filling fractions of HCN and CO (Phi_HCN/CO) are a significant source of uncertainty.

evidence.quote: A significant source of uncertainty instead comes from variations in the relative filling fractions of the HCN/CO transitions:

limitations_admitted.value: Magnetic fields are neglected (beta -> infinity), turbulent forcing is fixed at b = 0.4, local star formation efficiency is fixed at epsilon_0 = 1%, and the virial parameter alpha_vir is not independently varied in the LN models.

evidence.loc: Model Framework: Gravoturbulent Models of Star Formation
evidence.quote: Without a clear prescription for $\beta$ and $b$ in our sample, we simply take $\beta\rightarrow\infty$, which assumes that $B=0$ G. We take an intermediate value $b=0.4$, which assumes that turbulence is a mixture of compressive and solenoidal forcing.
One parameter that we did not vary in this analysis is $\alpha_\mathrm{vir}$.

referee_caveats_inferred: Physical resolution varies by nearly a factor of 20 across the ALMA sample (48 pc in M83 to 903 pc in VV114) and even more when compared to the 33'' single-dish EMPIRE sample, mixing individual GMC scales with kpc-scale galaxy-integrated regimes where beam averaging and rotational broadening dominate sigma_v.

Using a constant alpha_HCN/alpha_CO = 3.2 and constant alpha_CO = 1.1 across both normal spiral centers and extreme ULIRGs ignores known excitation and optical depth variations that directly affect both axes of plots involving f_dense, Sigma_mol, and P_turb.

P_turb (~ Sigma_mol * sigma_v^2) and t_ff (~ Sigma_mol^-0.5) share mathematical dependencies on I_CO with t_dep (~ I_CO / L_93GHz) and f_dense (~ I_HCN / I_CO), which can induce artificial correlations from correlated measurement noise or conversion factor variations.

data_public_as_stated.value: Archival ALMA data (16 project codes listed) and publicly-available EMPIRE survey single-dish data

evidence.quote: We compare the results of our sample with those of the EMPIRE survey (cite: Jimenez_Donaire:2019), for which there are publicly-available single-dish (IRAM 30m) observations of HCN and CO.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2011.0.00467.S,

missing_for_reproduction: Exact ALMA imaging parameters (uv-range matching limits, tapering parameters, robust weighting, cell size, cleaning thresholds) which are in Wilson et al. (submitted) or unstated for the 3 re-imaged galaxies
Tabulated pixel-by-pixel derived values or FITS moment maps for the 10 galaxies
Exact Spearman rank correlation coefficients (r_s) and chi^2 values, which are only plotted inside the figures rather than tabulated in the text
Definitions of the spatial masks used to exclude AGN-contaminated pixels in galaxies hosting an AGN
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Moderate (~50-200 GB for raw archival visibilities across 16 ALMA projects for 10 galaxies; <5 GB for reduced spectral cubes and continuum maps)
reproducibility.score_reason: All 16 archival ALMA project codes are explicitly listed, and the equations for moment maps, uncertainties, physical quantities, and analytical star formation models are fully specified in the text and Table 2. However, the visibility reduction and uv-matching/tapering details are deferred to a companion paper (Wilson et al., submitted at the time), AGN pixel masks are not quantitatively specified, and the numerical correlation/chi^2 values are only embedded in figure panels.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: While the archival data are public and the analytical model equations are complete, the main conclusions are qualitative model-data trend comparisons and graphical chi^2/Spearman evaluations rather than standalone numeric parameters, and the upstream cube imaging relies on an external companion paper.

methods_papers.why: Provides the LN PN11 gravoturbulent star formation formalism and turbulent density threshold prescription
Provides analytical equations for star formation efficiency per free-fall time and logarithmic density variance
Provides the composite lognormal plus powerlaw (LN+PL B18) n-PDF analytical formalism for epsilon_ff
Provides the transition density s_t and self-gravitating gas fraction f_grav equations for the LN+PL model
Provides the cube masking algorithm and the empirical cloud-scale sigma_v-Sigma_mol relation used to construct the model grid
Provides the composite thermal and non-thermal 93 GHz radio continuum SFR calibration
Provides the spectral resolution deconvolution formula for velocity dispersion

companion_papers.why: Presents the sample selection, ALMA data reduction and imaging, galaxy distances, and moment uncertainty derivations
Explores non-LTE radiative transfer modelling of HCN and CO emissivities, conversion factors, and beam filling fractions on a pixel-by-pixel basis for the same galaxy sample
Earlier study of the (U)LIRG subset establishing the double power-law Kennicutt-Schmidt relation and 93 GHz dust contribution
